{{short description|Oscillating dynamical system with nonlinear damping}}

In the study of [[dynamical system]]s, the '''van der Pol oscillator''' (named for Dutch physicist [[Balthasar van der Pol]]) is a non-[[Conservative force|conservative]], [[oscillating]] system with non-linear [[damping]]. It evolves in time according to the [[second-order differential equation]]
<math display=block>{d^2x \over dt^2}  - \mu(1-x^2){dx \over dt} +  x   =   0, </math>
where {{mvar|x}} is the position [[coordinate system|coordinate]]—which is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] of the time {{mvar|t}}—and {{mvar|μ}} is a [[scalar (mathematics)|scalar]] parameter indicating the [[nonlinearity]] and the strength of the damping.

[[File:Van der Pol oscillator phase plot 01.webm|thumb|van der Pol oscillator [[Phase portrait|phase plot]], with {{mvar|&mu;}} varying from 0.1 to 3.0. The green lines are the {{mvar|x}}-[[nullcline]]s.]]
[[File:Van der Pol oscillator phase plot Liénard transformation.webm|thumb|The same oscillator phase plot, but with [[Liénard equation#Example|Liénard transform]].]]
[[Image:Dynamics of the Van der Pol Oscillator.gif|thumb|The Van der Pol Oscillator simulated with the Brain Dynamics Toolbox<ref>Heitmann, S., Breakspear, M (2017–2022) Brain Dynamics Toolbox. [https://bdtoolbox.org bdtoolbox.org] [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5625923 doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5625923]</ref>]]
[[File:VanderPol-lc.svg|thumb|Evolution of the [[limit cycle]] in the [[phase plane]]. The limit cycle begins as a circle and, with varying {{mvar|μ}}, becomes increasingly sharp. An example of a [[relaxation oscillator]].]]

==History==
The Van der Pol oscillator was originally proposed by the Dutch [[electrical engineering|electrical engineer]] and physicist [[Balthasar van der Pol]] while he was working at [[Philips]].<ref name="Biography">{{cite journal |last=Cartwright |first=M. L. |year=1960 |title=Balthazar Van Der Pol |url=http://jlms.oxfordjournals.org/cgi/pdf_extract/s1-35/3/367 |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |publisher=Wiley |volume=s1-35 |issue=3 |pages=367–376 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-35.3.367 |issn=0024-6107|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Van der Pol found stable oscillations,<ref>B. van der Pol: "A theory of the amplitude of free and forced triode vibrations", Radio Review (later Wireless World) 1 701–710 (1920)</ref> which he subsequently called [[relaxation oscillator|relaxation-oscillations]]<ref name="relax">{{cite journal | last=van der Pol | first=Balth. | title=On "relaxation-oscillations" | journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science | publisher=Informa UK Limited | volume=2 | issue=11 | year=1926 | issn=1941-5982 | doi=10.1080/14786442608564127 | pages=978–992}}</ref> and are now known as a type of [[limit cycle]], in [[electrical circuit]]s employing [[vacuum tube]]s. When these circuits are driven near the [[limit cycle]], they become [[entrainment (physics)|entrained]], i.e. the driving [[signal (electrical engineering)|signal]] pulls the current along with it. Van der Pol and his colleague, van der Mark, reported in the September 1927 issue of ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' that at certain drive [[frequency|frequencies]] an irregular [[noise (electronic)|noise]] was heard,<ref name="Nature">{{cite journal | last1=VAN DER POL | first1=BALTH | last2=VAN DER MARK | first2=J. | title=Frequency Demultiplication | journal=Nature | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=120 | issue=3019 | year=1927 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/120363a0 | pages=363–364| bibcode=1927Natur.120..363V | s2cid=186244992 }}</ref> which was later found to be the result of [[chaos theory|deterministic chaos]].<ref>Kanamaru, T., [http://www.scholarpedia.org/article/Van_der_Pol_oscillator "Van der Pol oscillator"], ''[[Scholarpedia]]'', '''2'''(1), 2202, (2007).</ref>

The Van der Pol equation has a long history of being used in both the [[physical science|physical]] and [[biology|biological]] [[science]]s. For instance, in biology, Fitzhugh<ref name="fitz">{{cite journal | last=FitzHugh | first=Richard | title=Impulses and Physiological States in Theoretical Models of Nerve Membrane | journal=Biophysical Journal | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=1 | issue=6 | year=1961 | issn=0006-3495 | pmc=1366333| doi=10.1016/s0006-3495(61)86902-6 | pages=445–466| pmid=19431309 | bibcode=1961BpJ.....1..445F }}</ref> and Nagumo<ref name="nag">{{cite journal | last1=Nagumo | first1=J. | last2=Arimoto | first2=S. | last3=Yoshizawa | first3=S. | title=An Active Pulse Transmission Line Simulating Nerve Axon | journal=Proceedings of the IRE | publisher=Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) | volume=50 | issue=10 | year=1962 | issn=0096-8390 | doi=10.1109/jrproc.1962.288235 | pages=2061–2070| s2cid=51648050 }}</ref> extended the equation in a [[plane (mathematics)|planar field]] as a [[FitzHugh–Nagumo model|model]] for [[action potential]]s of [[neurons]]. The equation has also been utilised in [[seismology]] to model the two plates in a [[geological fault]],<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Cartwright | first1=Julyan H. E. |author-link = Julyan Cartwright| last2=Eguíluz | first2=Víctor M. | last3=Hernández-García | first3=Emilio | last4=Piro | first4=Oreste | title=Dynamics of Elastic Excitable Media | journal=International Journal of Bifurcation and Chaos | volume=09 | issue=11 | year=1999 | issn=0218-1274 | doi=10.1142/s0218127499001620|arxiv=chao-dyn/9905035 | pages=2197–2202| bibcode=1999IJBC....9.2197C | s2cid=9120223 }}</ref> and in studies of [[phonation]] to model the right and left [[Vocal folds|vocal fold]] oscillators.<ref>{{Cite conference|title = Modeling vocal fold asymmetries with coupled van der Pol oscillators|url = http://scitation.aip.org/content/asa/journal/poma/19/1/10.1121/1.4798467|conference = Proceedings of Meetings on Acoustics|date = 2013|issn = 1939-800X|page = 060165|volume = 19|issue = 1|doi = 10.1121/1.4798467|first1 = Jorge C.|last1 = Lucero|first2 = Jean|last2 = Schoentgen|url-access = subscription}}</ref>

== Two-dimensional form ==
[[Liénard's theorem]] can be used to prove that the system has a limit cycle. Applying the Liénard transformation <math>y = x - x^3/3 - \dot x/\mu</math>, where the dot indicates the time derivative, the Van der Pol oscillator can be written in its two-dimensional form:<ref>Kaplan, D. and Glass, L., ''Understanding Nonlinear Dynamics'', Springer, 240–244, (1995).</ref>
:<math>\dot x = \mu \left(x-\tfrac{1}{3}x^3-y\right)</math>
:<math>\dot y = \frac{1}{\mu} x</math>.

This form is also called the [[State-space representation#Nonlinear_systems|state space representation]].

Another commonly used form based on the transformation <math>y = \dot x </math> leads to:
:<math>\dot x = y</math>
:<math>\dot y = \mu(1-x^2) y-x</math>.

==Results for the unforced oscillator==
[[File:Vanderpol mu=5.svg|thumb|right|[[Relaxation oscillation]] in the Van der Pol oscillator without external forcing. The nonlinear damping parameter is equal to {{math|1=''μ'' = 5}}.]]
<ref>Grimshaw, R., ''Nonlinear ordinary differential equations'', [[CRC Press]], 153–163, (1993), {{ISBN|0-8493-8607-1}}.</ref>

* When {{math|1=''μ'' = 0}}, i.e. there is no damping function, the equation becomes<math display="block">
\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + x = 0.
</math>This is a form of the [[harmonic oscillator|simple harmonic oscillator]], and there is always [[conservation of energy]].

* When {{math|1=''μ'' > 0}}, all trajectories except the equilibrium at <math>x = \dot{x} = 0</math> approach a unique stable limit cycle.<ref>{{cite web |last=Dobrushkin |first=Vladimir |title=MATHEMATICA tutorial, Part 2.3: van der Pol |website=Brown University |url=https://www.cfm.brown.edu/people/dobrush/am34/Mathematica/ch3/pol.html |at=Theorem 1 |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref> Near the origin <math>x = \tfrac{dx}{dt} = 0,</math> the system is unstable, and far from the origin, the system is damped.
* The Van der Pol oscillator does not have an exact, analytic solution.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Panayotounakos | first1=D.E. | last2=Panayotounakou | first2=N.D. | last3=Vakakis | first3=A.F. | title=On the lack of analytic solutions of the Van der Pol oscillator | journal=ZAMM | publisher=Wiley | volume=83 | issue=9 | date=2003-09-01 | issn=0044-2267 | doi=10.1002/zamm.200310040 | pages=611–615| bibcode=2003ZaMM...83..611P | s2cid=120504403 }}</ref> However, such a solution does exist for the limit cycle if {{math|''f''(''x'')}} in the [[Lienard equation]] is a constant piece-wise function.
* The period at small {{mvar|&mu;}} has serial expansion <math display=block>
T = \frac{2\pi}{1- \mu^2/16 + 17 \mu^4/3072 + O(\mu^6)}.</math> See [[Poincaré–Lindstedt method]] for a derivation to order 2. See chapter 10 of <ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Verhulst |first=Ferdinand |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-642-61453-8 |title=Nonlinear Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems |date=1996 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-60934-6 |series=Universitext |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-61453-8}}</ref> for a derivation up to order 3, and <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Andersen |first1=C. M. |last2=Geer |first2=James F. |date=June 1982 |title=Power Series Expansions for the Frequency and Period of the Limit Cycle of the Van Der Pol Equation |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/0142047 |journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics |language=en |volume=42 |issue=3 |pages=678–693 |doi=10.1137/0142047 |issn=0036-1399|url-access=subscription }}</ref> for a numerical derivation up to order 164.
* For large {{mvar|&mu;}}, the behavior of the oscillator has a slow buildup, fast release cycle (a cycle of building up the tension and releasing the tension, thus a '''relaxation oscillation'''). This is most easily seen in the form <math display=block>
\dot x = \mu \left(x-\frac{1}{3}x^3-y\right) \! , \quad \dot y = \frac{1}{\mu} x.
</math> In this form, the oscillator completes one cycle as follows:
** Slowly ascending the right branch of the cubic curve <math>y = x - \tfrac{x^3}{3},</math> from {{math|(2, –2/3)}} to {{math|(1, 2/3)}}.
** Rapidly moving to the left branch of the cubic curve, from {{math|(1, 2/3)}} to {{math|(–2, 2/3)}}.
** Repeat the two steps on the left branch.
* The leading term in the period of the cycle is due to the slow ascending and descending, which can be computed as:<math display="block">
T = 2\int dt = 2\int \mu\frac{dy}{x} = 2\mu \int_2^1\frac{dy}{dx} \frac{dx}{x} = (3-2\ln 2)\mu
</math> Higher orders of the period of the cycle is <math display="block">
T = (3-2\ln 2)\mu + 3\alpha \mu^{-1/3} - \frac{22}{9\mu} \ln \mu + \frac{0.0087\cdots}{\mu} + O (\mu^{-4/3}).
</math> where {{math|''α'' ≈ 2.338}} is the smallest root of {{math|1=Ai(–''&alpha;'') = 0}}, where {{math|Ai}} is the [[Airy function]]. (Section 9.7 <ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last=Bender |first=Carl M. |title=Advanced mathematical methods for scientists and engineers I: asymptotic methods and perturbation theory |date=1999 |others=Steven A. Orszag |isbn=978-1-4757-3069-2 |location=New York, NY |oclc=851704808}}</ref>) (<ref>{{Cite book |last=Grimshaw |first=R. |title=Nonlinear ordinary differential equations |date=1993 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=0-8493-8607-1 |location=Boca Raton, Fla. |pages=161–163 |oclc=28275539}}</ref> contains a derivation, but has a misprint of {{math|3''&alpha;''}} to {{math|2''&alpha;''}}.) This was derived by [[Anatoly Dorodnitsyn]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=A |first=Dorodnicyn A. |date=1947 |title=Asymptotic solution of van der Pol's equation |url=https://archive.org/details/asymptoticsoluti2489doro/page/n5/mode/2up |journal=Prikl. Mat. Mech. |language=ru |volume=11 |pages=313–328}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Dorodnicyn |first=A. A. |url=http://archive.org/details/asymptoticsoluti2489doro |title=Asymptotic solution of Van Der Pol's equation |publisher=National Bureau of Standards |others=NIST Research Library}}</ref>
* The amplitude of the cycle is <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zonneveld |first=J.A. |date=1966 |title=Periodic solutions of the Van der Pol equation |journal=Indagationes Mathematicae (Proceedings) |volume=69 |pages=620–622 |doi=10.1016/s1385-7258(69)50068-x |issn=1385-7258|doi-access=free }}</ref> <math display="block">2 +\frac \alpha 3 \mu^{-4/3} - \frac{16}{27}\mu^{-2} \ln \mu + O(\mu^{-2})</math>

== Hopf bifurcation ==
As {{mvar|&mu;}} moves from less than zero to more than zero, the spiral sink at origin becomes a spiral source, and a limit cycle appears "out of the blue" with radius two. This is because the transition is not generic: when {{math|1=''&epsilon;'' = 0}}, both the differential equation becomes linear, and the origin becomes a circular node.

Knowing that in a [[Hopf bifurcation]], the limit cycle should have size <math>\propto \varepsilon^{1/2},</math> we may attempt to convert this to a Hopf bifurcation by using the change of variables <math>u = \varepsilon^{1/2} x,</math> which gives<math display="block">\ddot{u}+u+u^2 \dot{u}-\varepsilon \dot{u}=0</math>This indeed is a Hopf bifurcation.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Strogatz |first=Steven |title=Nonlinear dynamics and chaos: with applications to physics, biology, chemistry, and engineering |date=2019 |isbn=978-0-367-09206-1 |edition=2nd |location=Boca Raton |chapter=Example 8.4.1 |oclc=1112373147}}</ref>

==Hamiltonian for Van der Pol oscillator==
[[File:Attractors-Orbit.gif|250px|thumb|right|Randomly chosen initial conditions are attracted to a stable orbit.]]
One can also write a time-independent [[Hamiltonian system|Hamiltonian]] formalism for the Van der Pol oscillator by augmenting it to a four-dimensional autonomous dynamical system using an auxiliary second-order nonlinear differential equation as follows:

:<math>\ddot{x}-\mu(1-x^2)\dot{x}+x=0,</math>
:<math>\ddot{y}+\mu(1-x^2)\dot{y}+y=0.</math>

Note that the dynamics of the original Van der Pol oscillator is not affected due to the one-way coupling between the time-evolutions of ''x'' and ''y'' variables. A Hamiltonian ''H'' for this system of equations can be shown to be<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Conservative perturbation theory for nonconservative systems|url = https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.92.062927|journal = Physical Review E|date = 2015|article-number = 062927|volume = 92|issue = 6|first1 = Tirth|last1 = Shah|first2 = Rohitashwa|last2 = Chattopadhyay|first3 = Kedar|last3 = Vaidya|first4 = Sagar|last4 = Chakraborty|doi=10.1103/physreve.92.062927|pmid = 26764794|bibcode = 2015PhRvE..92f2927S|arxiv = 1512.06758|s2cid = 14930486}}</ref>

:<math>H(x,y,p_x,p_y)=p_xp_y+xy-\mu(1-x^2)yp_y, </math>

where <math>p_x=\dot{y} + \mu(1-x^2)y</math> and <math>p_y=\dot{x}</math> are the [[Canonical coordinates|conjugate momenta]] corresponding to ''x'' and ''y'', respectively. This may, in principle, lead to quantization of the Van der Pol oscillator. Such a Hamiltonian also connects<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Finding the Hannay angle in dissipative oscillatory systems via conservative perturbation theory|url = https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.97.062209|journal = Physical Review E|date = 2018|article-number = 062209|volume = 97|issue = 6|first1 = Rohitashwa|last1 = Chattopadhyay|first2 = Tirth|last2 = Shah|first3 = Sagar|last3 = Chakraborty|doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.97.062209|pmid = 30011548|arxiv = 1610.05218| bibcode=2018PhRvE..97f2209C |s2cid = 51635019}}</ref> the [[geometric phase]] of the limit cycle system having time dependent parameters with the [[Hannay angle]] of the corresponding Hamiltonian system.

===Quantum oscillator===
The quantum van der Pol oscillator, which is the [[quantum mechanical]] version of the classical van der Pol oscillator, has been proposed using a [[Lindblad equation]] to study its quantum dynamics and [[quantum synchronization]].<ref name="CKN20">{{cite journal | last1=Chia | first1=A. | last2=Kwek | first2=L. C. | last3=Noh | first3=C. | title=Relaxation oscillations and frequency entrainment in quantum mechanics | journal=Physical Review E | volume=102 | issue=4 | date=2020-10-16 | issn=2470-0045 | doi=10.1103/physreve.102.042213 | article-number=042213| pmid=33212685 | arxiv=1711.07376 | bibcode=2020PhRvE.102d2213C | s2cid=224801468 }}</ref> Note the above Hamiltonian approach with an auxiliary second-order equation produces unbounded phase-space trajectories and hence cannot be used to quantize the van der Pol oscillator. In the limit of weak nonlinearity (i.e. ''μ→''0) the van der Pol oscillator reduces to the [[Stuart–Landau equation]]. The Stuart–Landau equation in fact describes an entire class of limit-cycle oscillators in the weakly-nonlinear limit. The form of the classical Stuart–Landau equation is much simpler, and perhaps not surprisingly, can be quantized by a Lindblad equation which is also simpler than the Lindblad equation for the van der Pol oscillator. The quantum Stuart–Landau model has played an important role in the study of quantum synchronisation<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Walter | first1=Stefan | last2=Nunnenkamp | first2=Andreas | last3=Bruder | first3=Christoph | title=Quantum Synchronization of a Driven Self-Sustained Oscillator | journal=Physical Review Letters | volume=112 | issue=9 | date=2014-03-06 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.112.094102 | article-number=094102| pmid=24655255 | arxiv=1307.7044 | bibcode=2014PhRvL.112i4102W | s2cid=7950471 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Lee | first1=Tony E. | last2=Sadeghpour | first2=H. R. | title=Quantum Synchronization of Quantum van der Pol Oscillators with Trapped Ions | journal=Physical Review Letters | volume=111 | issue=23 | date=2013-12-04 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.111.234101 | article-number=234101| pmid=24476274 | arxiv=1306.6359 | bibcode=2013PhRvL.111w4101L | s2cid=33622111 }}</ref> (where it has often been called a van der Pol oscillator although it cannot be uniquely associated with the van der Pol oscillator). The relationship between the classical Stuart–Landau model (''μ→''0) and more general limit-cycle oscillators (arbitrary ''μ'') has also been demonstrated numerically in the corresponding quantum models.<ref name="CKN20" />

==Forced Van der Pol oscillator==
[[File:Vanderpol time mu=8.53 A=1.2 T=10.svg|thumb|right|[[Chaos theory|Chaotic behaviour]] in the Van der Pol oscillator with sinusoidal forcing. The nonlinear damping parameter is equal to {{math|1=''μ'' = 8.53}}, while the forcing has amplitude {{math|1=''A'' = 1.2}} and angular frequency {{math|1=''ω'' = 2π/10}}.]]
The forced, or driven, Van der Pol oscillator takes the 'original' function and adds a driving function {{math|''A''sin(''ωt'')}} to give a differential equation of the form:

:<math>{d^2x \over dt^2}-\mu(1-x^2){dx \over dt}+x   =   A \sin(\omega t),</math>

where {{mvar|A}} is the [[amplitude]] of the [[sine wave|sinusoidal]] driving function and {{mvar|ω}} is its [[angular frequency]].

==Popular culture==
[[File:Van der pol triode.svg|thumb|right|[[Electrical circuit]] involving a [[triode]], resulting in a forced Van der Pol oscillator.<ref name=Tomita>K. Tomita (1986): "Periodically forced nonlinear oscillators". In: ''Chaos'', Ed. Arun V. Holden. Manchester University Press, {{ISBN|0719018110}}, pp. 213–214.</ref>  The circuit contains: a triode, a [[resistor]] ''R'', a [[capacitor]] ''C'', a coupled [[inductor]]-set with [[self inductance]] ''L'' and [[mutual inductance]] ''M''.  In the serial [[RLC circuit]] there is a current ''i'', and towards the triode [[anode]] ("plate") a current ''i<sub>a</sub>'', while there is a voltage ''u<sub>g</sub>'' on the triode [[control grid]]. The Van der Pol oscillator is forced by an AC [[voltage source]] ''E<sub>s</sub>''.]]
Author [[James Gleick]] described a [[vacuum tube]] Van der Pol oscillator in his book from 1987 ''[[Chaos: Making a New Science]]''.<ref name=gleick-chaos>{{cite book|last=Gleick|first=James|title=Chaos: Making a New Science|year=1987|publisher=Penguin Books|location=New York|isbn=0-14-009250-1|pages=41–43}}</ref>  According to a ''[[New York Times]]'' article,<ref name=colman-nyt>{{cite news|last=Colman|first=David|title=There's No Quiet Without Noise|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/07/10/fashion/a-machine-designed-to-add-chaos-to-order.html|access-date=11 July 2011|newspaper=New York Times|date=11 July 2011}}</ref> Gleick received a modern electronic Van der Pol oscillator from a reader in 1988.
